Coin Change

CountingAlgorithmsArithmetic
Game: There is no winner here: discover how many different ways a pile of money can be made from the coins you pick.
How to play: Tick the coins you want, type an amount, and press Compute. Click a bar or use the arrow keys to read any amount.

Coins you may use
Look for the math

Hand someone a handful of coins and ask them to make a certain amount. There can be far more ways than you expect, and the trick that counts them all is surprisingly small.

What counts as a way

Only the coins matter, not the order you hand them over. Making 6 from a 5 and a 1 is the same as making it from a 1 and a 5, so it counts once. This is a combination, and it is why we may use each kind of coin as many times as we like without worrying about the sequence.

A polynomial that counts

A coin of value d can be used 0, 1, 2, ... times, which contributes the factor 1 + xd + x2d + ⋯. Multiply one such factor for every coin you chose. In the product, the coefficient of xn is exactly the number of ways to change n. That product is called a generating function:

(1 + xd₁ + x2d₁ + ⋯)(1 + xd₂ + ⋯) = ⋯ + wn xn + ⋯

Each time you take a term xkd from a factor you are saying "use k coins of value d", and the exponents add up to the amount you are making.

How the applet multiplies

The applet kept each factor as a list with a 1 wherever the power is a multiple of d and 0 elsewhere. Multiplying two lists adds up shifted copies of one of them — a convolution, its GeoPoly.Times method. This page uses the same idea as a running sum: start with w(0) = 1, then for each coin d add w(n − d) into w(n). The logic test compares the two over every one of the 256 coin choices and every amount up to 120; they agree.

A quirk with big counts

The original applet stored its counts in 64-bit whole numbers, which wrap around when the amount is large and many coins are chosen, so the displayed number becomes wrong. This page keeps exact integers instead. The page itself states no formula to check — only the question "in how many ways ...", which the chart answers. With the default coins 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 there are 292 ways to change 100, a classic result the test confirms.

Tick the 2 coin and watch the counts grow, then untick the 1 coin: suddenly some amounts cannot be made at all.
